summary: Design-science study at Ericsson: a Kiro CLI orchestrator dispatches four parallel sub-agents (readability, maintainability, reliability, performance), each with its own skill document and antipattern catalog, fed by a context builder that pulls diffs from a GitLab MCP server and dependency structure from a code-knowledge-graph MCP server. Run on 7 commits from 4 Python projects, it produced 206 issues; the commits' developers rated 197 (96%) correct and 69% of those medium/high importance.

claims.claim: The solution achieves 96% accuracy in identifying issues.
claims.evidence: Table 7: 197/206 correct. This is precision as judged by the commits' own developers; recall (issues missed) is not measured; 5 raters, one of whom rated 96 of 206 issues (§3.3); no inter-rater agreement.

claims.claim: About 69% of correct issues are important (33% must-fix, 36% should-fix).
Contextual grounding via the code knowledge graph explains the low false-positive rate.
claims.evidence: Attribution only; §5.1 states no ablation or comparison with alternative designs was performed, so this is feasibility evidence.

claims.claim: Decomposing review into dimension-specific agents yields broader coverage than a single-dimension review.
claims.evidence: Table 6 distribution (reliability 31.1%, readability 28.2%, maintainability 24.3%, performance 16.5%); no single-agent multi-dimension baseline was run, so the claim that one review 'would have covered at most about a third' is tautological.

patterns.note: LLM reviewer findings were mostly judged correct and important by developers in an industrial setting; precision only, no recall or comparison with human review.
Role-specialized review agents; no ablation against a single agent.
Specialist agents run as parallel sub-agents each receiving a tailored context view.
Agent Skills documents carry each agent's antipattern checklist.
GitLab and code-knowledge-graph access via containerized MCP servers.
Code knowledge graph (imports, DEFINES edges, fan-in/fan-out, cross-repo search) supplies structural context; benefit asserted, not isolated.
Real industrial commits rated by their developers, albeit tiny sample.

methodology.sample: 7 commits from 4 projects (2 small, 2 large) at one company; 206 issues; 5 senior-developer raters; 3 practitioners in problem identification.
methodology.baselines: None (no human-review, single-agent, or no-context baseline).
methodology.models: Single LLM: Kiro CLI's default model (not named).
methodology.variance: Not measured; non-determinism acknowledged as a threat.

standards.peer_review: Accepted at PROFES 2026 (27th Int. Conf. on Product-Focused Software Process Improvement).
standards.artifacts: Antipattern catalogs and feedback template reported in paper; commits, reviews, and agent configs proprietary.

biases.detail: 7 commits, 4 projects, 5 raters; one rater covers 47% of issues.
Unnamed Kiro CLI default model only.
'Accuracy' is precision; recall and missed defects are not assessed.
Raters are the code authors, who may be lenient or strict; no inter-rater reliability; Ericsson co-author on the paper.
No token, time or cost data for four parallel agents plus orchestration.
Qualitative feedback limited to two positive quotes.

coi.affiliations: Blekinge Institute of Technology (Laiq, Usman, Britto, Badampudi); Ericsson AB (Britto, Saini).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Authors' own in-house prototype built on Kiro CLI (third-party AWS tool), evaluated at their own company.
coi.funding: Knowledge Foundation, InScale project (20230095) at BTH; no competing interests declared.
coi.detail: Industry-academic collaboration evaluating its own prototype internally; no commercial product being promoted.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed real industrial evaluation with honest threats section, but tiny sample, precision-only metric, no baseline or ablation, one unnamed model, Python only, and closed artifacts.
applicability: Relevant as an architectural template, weak as evidence. The setup (orchestrator + per-dimension review sub-agents defined declaratively as skills + GitLab MCP + a cross-repository code-graph MCP) maps closely to what a Java team could run across its several repositories, and the declarative JSON+markdown agent definitions are host-portable in spirit (Kiro here; similar skills work in Claude Code/Cursor), which suits mixed hosts. But the 96% figure is precision on Python commits rated by their authors; the team should expect to re-measure on Java with recall (seeded defects or past incidents) before trusting it as a gate, and should keep LLM review advisory behind deterministic checks (tests, Sonar/Semgrep) under spec-driven development.

conflicts_with.detail: That paper argues coding agents supersede human inspection; this study keeps humans as the judges of AI review findings and measures only precision, so it does not support replacing human review.
